en: Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Chapters 1–3 (Missing) The Profound and Subtle Succession of Names ...the mark of the signless...
By reciting the name together with [the practice of] □□□□□□□, one gives rise to □□; it is not found outside.
This is because it is precisely □□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□, and not something external.
Therefore, because it accords with reality, it is titled the "Chapter on Names and Epithets" (Nam-hyo-pin). [Omission].

Chapter Four: The Four Noble Truths (Sa-je-pin). Regarding this chapter, the sequence from beginning to end—[omission]—may be understood from the text according to the subsequent listing of the names and epithets of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The purport of its characteristics is... [lacuna].
Chapter Five: The Awakening of Radiance (*Prabhāsa-bodhi*). As for the reason this chapter is presented:
The preceding two chapters extensively elucidate the characteristics of the principles and their underlying intent,
correctly clarifying the state of Buddhahood:
its realization of reality and its wondrous function pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
However, as these meanings encompass profound moisture and entrustment, they cannot be fathomed through mere subtle insight;
one must rely on the supernatural power of the Great Sage’s spiritual path to perceive even a slight semblance of them,
thereby finding a place for the mind to rest.
Therefore, the Tathāgata emits a great radiance from the *cakra* on the sole of his foot,
manifesting the mark of reality so that all beings with hearts capable of receiving it are awakened.
For this reason, the first chapter is titled "The Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance."
6. Chapter on Clarifying Objections (Mingnanpin), Chapter Six.

The reason this chapter is presented is that while the preceding "Chapter on the Manifestation of Radiant Enlightenment" demonstrated the verification of direct realization, it did not yet address the reality of the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of perfect enlightenment and quiescent extinction.
Yet it is manifested within the chapter titled "The Dharma-realm.
Now, as for the designation "Dharma-realm," it is the characteristic of the characteristicless.
The reality of their mutual identity is such that it is also like this for the ocean of sentient beings.
This principle is profound and subtle, the most difficult among difficulties.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, together with the great bodhisattvas of the various directions, has carefully examined your traces and set forth ten types of gates of inquiry.
Because each point is explained according to its meaning so that the profound purport of the correct answers may be revealed, it is called the "Chapter on Clarifying Difficulties.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Pure Conduct. As for the reason this chapter is presented:
The preceding section clarified that the sublime and wondrous fruition is not a cause that does not correspond to its causes;
for although it is immeasurable, there is nothing therein that is not pure conduct.
Next, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" is explained.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Bhadramukha. The reason this chapter is presented is that Mañjuśrī has already clarified the essential purity of practice.
Because the characteristics of its vast and profound meaning had not yet been revealed therein,
the "Chapter on the Wise Leader" (Bhadramukha-parivarta) is explained next as the eighth, so that the Wise Leader may expound its mysteries.
Chapter Nine: The Buddha Ascends the Summit of Mount Sumeru. The reason this chapter is presented is that the preceding section elucidated the true virtues of the Buddha’s fruition.
This concludes the brief exposition on the path of returning through skillful means to realize the fruit. Hereafter,
it further clarifies that the Tathāgata is supremely quiescent and ethereally concentrated, yet his activity pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
How is this known?
For it was not from the Bodhi tree that [the Way] arose for the six heavens;
rather, it is likewise so throughout the ten directions.

Because he subsequently wishes to extensively distinguish the stages of bodhisattva practice, which constitute the true and essential means for transcending existence, he next clarifies the "Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru.
Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Gathering of Bodhisattvas. As for the reason this chapter is presented:
The preceding section elucidated the aspect of the ten directions and the dharma-realm as a single, unified whole.
This chapter seeks to clarify that all things are equally true quiescence;
therefore, there are ten bodhisattvas who are Great Beings.
To observe all things according to reality and exhaustively penetrate the profound mystery is what is called "seeing the Buddha," wherein all discrimination is extinguished. Why is this so?
It is because one seeks to clarify that when a bodhisattva resolves to attain bodhicitta, they are definitively no different from a Buddha.
Next is the clarification of the "Chapter on the Gathering of Clouds.
Chapter Eleven: The Ten Abodes of the Bodhisattva. As for the reason this chapter is presented:
the preceding section clarified that true quiescence is signless and wondrously transcends all discrimination, thereby opening the perfect path to enlightenment for the Mahāsattvas.
Therefore, there is a mind that understands its course;
having first given rise to the great vow, the mind merges with the Great Quiescence, remaining firm and immovable.
This is called "abiding. Thus it is said.
Next is the explanation of the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes.

Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on Holy Conduct (*Brahmacarya*). The reason this chapter is presented is that the preceding section clarified how the mind merges with the Great Quiescence, remaining firm and unmoving, thereby fulfilling the meaning of "abiding" (*vihāra*).
This clarifies the definitive collection of the realization and cultivation of reality,
because one attains perfect awakening at the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta.
Next, the Chapter on the Holy Life (Brahmacarya) is clarified.

Chapter Thirteen: On Merit (Guǒdé Pǐn). The reason this chapter is presented is that the preceding section clarified that the holy life (brahmacarya) is the ultimate tranquility and the essence of reality.
This chapter elucidates that merit constitutes the adornment of skillful means.
While the preceding section demonstrated that the essence of practice is pure and equal,
this section reveals the significance of its manifold applications, wherein merits are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Next is the explanation of the Chapter on Merit.
Chapter Fourteen: The Explanation of the Dharma. The reason this chapter is presented is that the preceding sections have clarified the essence of the merit of the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya).
Since the meaning is vast and extensive, and one’s realization accords with that of the Buddha,
one should proceed toward excellence. Therefore,
Prajñākūṭa asked Dharmakīrti about the path of transcendent progress and superior advancement, which he explained in detail.
Because its characteristics are clearly manifested, it is called the "Chapter on the Dharma of Illumination.
Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on Sovereignty in Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. As for the reason this chapter is presented:
The preceding explanation of the twelve kinds of dharmas constitutes the path of supreme progress;
it is intended to manifest the heroic Great Being.
Because the profound mind attains mystical union without relying on gradual stages, the following clarifies the "Chapter on Sovereignty" in the Palace of Yāma. Chapter Sixteen:
The Bodhisattva’s Discourse in Verse. This discourse in verse shares a similar intent, dharma-application, purport, and metaphorical illustration with what preceded it.
The distinctions lie solely in the names, practices, stages, and positions;
this may be understood by reference to what precedes.
Chapter Seventeen: The Ten Practices (Daśacaryā-varga). What are the distinguishing characteristics of these ten practices compared to the preceding ten abodes?
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) clarify the correspondence between clear understanding and the resolve of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*).
Now, these ten practices clarify the meaning of establishing the conduct that proceeds toward and awaits [enlightenment]. How is this known?
Now, understanding arises from practice, and practice is perfected through understanding;
that understanding and practice are mutually requisite is a matter of natural principle.
This is because it constitutes the sequence of their initial arousal.
Furthermore, it is said that "understanding and practice" (jixing) refer to the stage [of realization].
This is what is meant by the principle of the true luminosity of one's nature.
When contemplation and understanding are perfectly aligned, they merge into a single, unified standard.
Because one faces the ocean of the dharma-realm with profound vastness and without fixed attachment, it is called "practice through understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*);
it is also termed "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).
This does not imply any difference in temporal sequence.
Now, as for speech and conduct:
one who embodies the Way and returns to the source, whose mind rests in empty stillness, and who already harbors benevolence within, will achieve progress and penetration in all things.
Even if one were to unleash lightning across the wilderness of the eight directions, [the power of such a person remains unsurpassed].

Just as they are not fettered by non-conditions, their compassionate light shines equally throughout the ten directions, unifying the myriad vehicles; in an instant, they grasp all phenomena within a single thought-moment, remaining unmoving.
It is like the King of Great Mountains, which is constantly ablaze.
The specific characteristics of such a profound meaning are beyond measure. Why is this?
The Buddhas have exhaustively expounded the initial generation of the mind in the first ten stages;
how much more so for the establishment of these practices once they are perfected?
How could names and words ever fully encompass their categories?
The sequence of their mutual connection is identical in meaning to that of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*);
the only difference lies in the stages of practice.
Chapter 18: The Chapter on the Ten Treasuries (*Daśakośa-varga*). Regarding the purpose for which this chapter is presented:

The preceding section distinguished the ten practices because they transcend and ascend, reaching the ultimate pinnacle and penetrating to the point where all is fused and unimpeded; thus, the mind merges with the true realm, the ocean of the *dharmadhātu-garbha*.
Therefore, it clarifies the ten kinds of inexhaustible treasuries in order to perfect the ten kinds of practices distinguished above.
Therefore, the meaning of the ten kinds of treasuries (kośa) is further elucidated.
The ten treasuries are: first, the treasury of faith (śraddhā-kośa).
The second is the treasury of ethical discipline;
the third is the treasury of self-respect;
and the fourth is the treasury of moral dread.
The fifth is the treasury of hearing;
the sixth is the treasury of giving;
the seventh is the treasury of wisdom.
The eighth is the treasury of right mindfulness;
the ninth is the treasury of retention;
the tenth is the treasury of discernment.
These are the ten. Now,
as for what is called a "treasury" (piṭaka),
it is essentially a name for the ocean of the Dharma.
Why is it called a "Treasury" (garbha)?
It is because its fundamental principle (*mūla*) encompasses all that is not subsumed, and its meaning (*artha*) embraces all that is not contained;
it is complete in its manifold capacities and its principles and characteristics are eternally thus. Therefore, it is called a Treasury.
Therefore, it is next titled "The Chapter on the Ten Stores.
Chapter Nineteen: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. As for the reason this chapter is presented:
The preceding section has distinguished the ten kinds of treasuries of the ocean;

it clarifies that when principle and practice first achieve superior progress, the wondrous true understanding transcends the stage of understanding-and-practice, and as the path of skillful means is perfected within the dark realm, the untainted state of direct realization manifests spontaneously.
Therefore, the destiny of a lifetime is entrusted [to this] to manifest its meaning; thus it is explained next. (20) [Missing] 21.
Regarding the thematic structure of the Chapter on the Ten Dedications (*Daśa-pariṇāmanā*) and the Chapter on Praise (*Stuti*): as for why this chapter was composed, [it is as follows].
The above clarifies the perfection of practice.
Because practice is supported by principle, true understanding cannot be manifested without practice;
thus, understanding and practice are harmoniously integrated, establishing the path to Bodhi. One then makes a vow to share this with all sentient beings.
Although the fruit of Buddhahood has not yet been fully realized, one does not abide in the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*).
Therefore, even a single hair’s breadth of merit naturally flows toward the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Next, the Chapter on Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is explained.
Within these ten dedications, there are three sections.
The first three clarify dedication in terms of phenomena (*dharma*);
the next three clarify dedication based on the path (*mārga*).
Regarding the latter three, they clarify the direction toward the vehicle.
As for the tenth, the "Infinite Dharma Realm," it is the complete fulfillment and accomplishment of the practices of the ocean-like Dharma realm, embodying the three aforementioned meanings.
Because the meaning of realizing the goal cannot be fully exhausted by words, it is called the "Infinite Dedication of the Dharma-realm.
Chapter Twenty-two: The Ten Stages. As for the reason this chapter is presented:

In the preceding section on dedication, it was clarified that the Great Being understands the profound source, such that there is not a single dharma upon which he can give rise to volitional thought or perform mental effort;
even so, he does not perceive a single characteristic that can be maintained.

Therefore, because their practice is perfected, their grace transcendent, and they have achieved the realization of the principle, all that manifests through the activity of their minds is entirely [the Dharma]; for this reason, it is explained next.
As for what is called "ground" (bhūmi):
He is determined to generate the Buddha-knowledge that sustains and maintains [the world].
Furthermore, by constantly giving rise to the four kinds of great wisdom, he bestows upon and transforms sentient beings.
Moreover, he personally establishes the five kinds of Nārāyaṇa banners.
For this reason, it is called "ground" (*bhūmi*).
Therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds. 23.
Chapter Twenty-three: The Ten Illuminations (*daśa-vidyā*). Regarding why this chapter was composed:
The preceding section has distinguished the virtues and conduct of the Mahāsattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which are so vast as to be unsurpassed and complete in every respect.
Taking the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as their body and universal illumination as their function,
they have attained full and thorough mastery over all phenomena.
To clarify this meaning, the "Chapter on the Ten Clarities" (Daśavidyā-varga) is subsequently analyzed.
Within it, the general purport does not exceed the three types of higher knowledge (trividyā), which are expanded into ten by means of the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā). How is this known?
The concluding summary states:
"When a bodhisattva dwells in this [stage], they fully attain the unimpeded wisdom and illumination regarding the three periods of time.
Within this, each point may be understood by explaining its meaning in detail."
The first is called the clear knowledge of knowing the minds of others,
by which one thoroughly understands the distinctions among the mental characteristics of all sentient beings.
The second is the unimpeded clear knowledge of the divine eye.
The Tathāgata’s sphere of activity is such that he can see entirely all instances of transmigrating from death here to birth there;
this is the third [supernormal knowledge]: the unimpeded supernormal knowledge of the clear realization of past lives reaching back to the limit of the past.
Transcending the light, one goes to all sentient beings, all matters, and the seats of all Buddhas and the seats of Bodhisattvas beneath the Bodhi tree;
even unto the perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas from their initial generation of the mind through their practice.
Up until the attainment of nirvana without remainder,
they are able to fully comprehend all phenomena;
they further enter deeply into the unimpeded wisdom-light regarding kalpas extending to the limits of the future.
The preceding section merely clarified the turning of the Tathāgata’s sphere of activity;
this [section] states that he is able to fully comprehend all matters.
All things throughout the entirety of future ages are the same as those of the past.
Fifth is the clear knowledge of the unimpeded, pure divine ear,
which is able to hear and know all sounds throughout the ten directions, even down to their phrases and meanings, without ever failing or losing them.
The sixth is the light of wisdom that abides securely in the power of fearlessness;
this is the characteristic of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
The seventh is the light of wisdom that discriminates all speech and sounds.
The eighth is the light of wisdom that produces the adornment of immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) form-bodies.
The ninth is the light of wisdom regarding the reality of all phenomena.
The tenth is the light of wisdom regarding the definitive nature of all phenomena.

Chapter Twenty-Four: The Ten Patiences. The reason this chapter is presented is that the preceding section has distinguished the clarity of perfect illumination and its thorough penetration of all phenomena.
This reveals the true understanding of abiding correctly in equanimity within non-arising and settling the mind;
in principle, this is termed "patience" (*kṣānti*).
Because it is elucidated according to its characteristics, it is called the "Chapter on the Ten Patiences."

Chapter Twenty-five: On the Incalculable (*Asaṃkhyeya*). The reason this chapter is presented is that, as discussed extensively above, the virtues of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are vast, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
All are described as *asaṃkhyeya*,
even up to "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*);
yet, while these serve to illustrate the extent of his practice, they do not explain the underlying reason.
Therefore, because the Tathāgata expounds this meaning, it is clarified next.
Chapter Twenty-Six: On Life Span. The reason this chapter is presented is as follows:
The excellence of his virtuous conduct, as explained above, is so vast that it cannot be fully described.

One wishes to clarify that virtue completes the person, and through this, one establishes the human law and brings the Way to fulfillment, its influence extending without end. Since both virtue and the Way are inexhaustible, [the teaching] is likewise boundless.
The meaning of "life-span" (*āyus*) is likewise the same.
For this reason, the "Chapter on Life-span" follows next.
Chapter Twenty-seven: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Abodes. The reason this chapter is introduced is as follows:
To clarify that the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of virtuous conduct and lifespan is neither middle nor extreme, and that the Dharma-body is equal, abiding by means of non-abiding,
the following "Chapter on the Abodes of the Bodhisattva" is explained.

Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Inconceivability of the Buddha-Dharma. The reason this chapter is presented is that, as explained extensively above, the virtuous conduct of the Bodhisattva is already inconceivable.
Yet, the meaning of the merits of all Buddhas remains unknown.
For what reason? Next, the "Inconceivable Chapter" is further elucidated.
Among these, regarding the eight kinds of sounds from which the Tathāgata is free:
first is the Brahma-voice;
second is the profound voice.
The third is "distant sound.
These three constitute the essence of sound.
The subsequent three are explained by way of analogy.
First, it is like the sound of a drum;
its resonance is grand and melodic.
Second, it is like the sound of seeds being sown.
The resonance of its sound is brilliant,
like the threefold tinkling of golden bells;
its tone is clear and distinct.
There are two other sounds of doubt:
first, the sound of a bird;
second, the sound of a "three-footed" bird.

Chapter Twenty-nine: The Ocean of Marks. This chapter is presented here simultaneously because the inconceivable nature of the Buddha-dharma discussed above is intended to clarify that its essence is harmoniously integrated and unimpeded.

This so-called "ocean" is intended to clarify that because characteristics are without exception unreal and fused without obstruction, there is no essence that is not meaning; because characteristics are without exception unreal, there is no meaning that is not essence; because essence is without exception meaning, one essence is all essences; and because meaning is without exception essence, one meaning is all meanings.
Therefore, essence is without the characteristic of essence, and meaning is without the characteristic of meaning; essence and meaning are fused.
Within these various functions of this and that, there is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic.
Now, based on the true mark (*dharmatā*) to manifest sublime virtue, it is called the "Chapter on the Ocean of Marks."
Chapter 30: On the Minor Characteristics (Xiaoxiang-pin). This chapter differs from the preceding one; it is a distinct title.
"Good" (*hao*) refers to following conditions (*yuan*);
thus, to manifest them is called "characteristics" (*xiang*), and to contemplate their essence is called "suchness" (*ru*).
Based on this principle, because it distinguishes itself from the "Small Chapter" (*Kṣudraka-varga*), it is called the "Chapter on Minor Characteristics" (*Kṣudra-lakṣaṇa-varga*).
**Chapter Thirty-one: The Conduct of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.** As for the reason why this chapter is presented:
The preceding section clarified that the merit of the fruition is equal to the ocean of the Dharma-realm, being neither central nor boundless.
Were it not for the perfect cause reaching its ultimate limit at the boundary of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), by what means could one possibly accord with it?
Therefore, since the perfect fruition has already been manifested, the perfect cause must likewise be revealed; hence, it is explained next.
It may also be said that this is the fruit-practice (phala-caryā) whose name is manifested by means of its reliance on the causal stage. Why is this so?
Its measure pervading the dharma-realm is called "universal" (prabhūta).
Its ultimate accord, harmony, and gentleness are termed "virtuous" (bhadra).
Because it is the application of the path to enlightenment, it is called "practice" (caryā). Thus, it is named the Universal-Virtuous-Practice Samādhi.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva":
Chapter Thirty-Two, "The Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata as the Jewel King. As for the reason this chapter is presented:
The preceding section has extensively distinguished the perfect cause and the perfect fruit.
Regarding the principle that the perfect cause accords with reality and the perfect fruit extends to the furthest limit— the profound intent of the excellence of cause and effect—
it is what is called "true nature" (bhūtatathatā).
Therefore, the meaning of the Arising of Nature (xingqi) is explained next.
However, while the functioning of nature has not yet arisen as suchness, the true nature remains eternally as it is throughout past and present.
This is because the functioning of nature arises constantly.
It is active yet profoundly quiescent,
for its true nature has remained thus throughout all time;
it is quiescent yet manifests through metaphorical expression.
Since quiescence and function are free from obstruction,
how could there be any dharmas of defilement or purity to be apprehended?
Therefore, true nature is the source of both opposition and conformity.
The fundamental wondrous function of the causal aggregation arises through it, while delusive appearances cease through it; thus, arising and ceasing emerge from deluded sentiment.
As for me, I have never acted, yet I act without acting; because there is nothing that is not being done.
The term "Jewel King Arising from Nature" (xingqi baowang) is a metaphorical illustration.
That which is sovereign and at will is called a "Jewel King";
true nature is likewise so.
The Tathāgata is called "Tathāgata" because he reveals the nature through its perfect manifestation;
therefore, this is titled the "Chapter on the Arising of the Nature of the Jewel-King Tathāgata.
Chapter Thirty-Three: The Chapter on Transcending the World. The reason this chapter is presented is as follows:
The preceding section has clarified that true nature is extinguished within all phenomena, which are entirely empty and quiescent;
the myriad marks return to the source, where perfect luminosity shines alone.
If there were only quiescence without arising, it would be identical to the great void;
how, then, could it constitute the true luminosity of the essential nature?
For this reason, the meaning is further clarified.
The dharmadhātu manifests its functions equally throughout the future; because it is equipped with manifold capacities, it is called the "world.
That no characteristic can be apprehended is termed "detachment" (*viveka*).
It is not that there exists some existent phenomenon (*bhāva*) which is to be detached from that is called detachment.
Therefore, it is titled "The Chapter on Departing from the World.

Chapter Thirty-Four: Entering the Dharma Realm. As for the reason this chapter is presented: the preceding sections have elucidated the functional significance of the Dharma Realm and its manifestations extending to the future limit.
If one does not abide [in this state], what benefit is there even if it be sublime?
Therefore, next, the entry into the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is explained.
Because its principles and meanings mutually encompass one another, it is designated by the name "dharma-realm."
To dissolve into true stillness is called "entry";
to accord with unimpeded function is named "practice.
Such a one is a true child of the Buddha, who succeeds to the lineage of the Triple Gem.
Because it establishes the meaning of uninterrupted circulation, it is named the "Entering the Dharma Realm" Chapter.
Regarding the Text of the Four Great Vows: Awakening is difficult to enter; therefore, one must summon its fulfillment through vows.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [upon enlightenment]...
Desiring to depart from evil and cultivate goodness, to extensively transform sentient beings and seek the fruit of Buddhahood afar,
one must take the great vow as the foundation.
Once the great vow is established, [the path proceeds].
Then one's wishes shall be fulfilled without exception,
just as the Buddha has praised:
through the power of the Tathāgata’s great wisdom, his proclaimed merits, his realization of patience, his wisdom, his meritorious deeds, and the power of his vows.
The single vow of the most excellent bodhisattva surpasses the practice of the śrāvakas for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
The practices and vows of a bodhisattva are indeed immeasurable;
these four are cited here as a brief illustration.
This encompasses them all completely. What are the four?
First, I, your disciple [Name].
I vow to sever all afflictions.
The Buddha-dharma is exceedingly profound; I pray that I may exhaust its very source and depths.
It is called "profound" because it eternally abides in the principle of the two truths, whose nature and characteristics are subtle and mysterious.
I vow that by exhausting the source of principle and severing delusions until they are utterly exhausted,
even though I do not yet sever them, the power of my great vows shall be so strong that in every place of rebirth, all afflictions will naturally diminish.
Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of two ways of cultivating the mind:
though one constantly possesses afflictions, they are as if non-existent;
this is the first vow.
Second, one vows to cultivate all meritorious virtues.
Though birth and death are fearsome, one aspires to always dwell within them;
just as people of the world cannot obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel unless they enter the ocean.
If a bodhisattva does not enter the ocean of the subjects of birth and death,
they cannot obtain the jewel of the unconditioned Buddha-fruition. Therefore,
the Great Being forms the aspiration for the most supreme and exalted fruit.
Entering birth and death to extensively cultivate the myriad practices,
one disregards all sufferings, vowing to take them as seeds that encompass all practices.
In every place of rebirth, all roots of goodness are spontaneously gathered and harvested, increasing in accordance with one’s vows.
This is the second vow.
Third, he vows to deliver all sentient beings;
though sentient beings are boundless, he vows to bring them all to liberation.
Abandon enmity toward enemies and abandon attachment toward kin;
treat enemy and kin with equal impartiality.
He extensively practices the four means of integration,
vowing that all sentient beings of the dharma realm shall simultaneously attain Buddhahood;
having abandoned the distinction between enemies and kin, he universally practices great compassion.
All enmity, poison, and evil intentions shall naturally perish.
Through internal cultivation of goodness, one is born into the family of the Buddha, possessing a noble lineage beyond reproach or disparagement.
This is the third vow.
Fourth, one vows to deliver all beings to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Although the path of the Buddha is long and distant,
it shall certainly be attained.
Ultimately, one does not give rise to a sense of complacency by considering the nirvana of the two vehicles as superior to the fruits of the mundane world; rather,
all roots of goodness throughout the three periods of time are dedicated toward unexcelled bodhi,
without calculating the number of kalpas required.
I vow to take the attainment of Buddhahood as my ultimate goal.
Since my aspirations are so lofty and far-reaching,
I do not expect worldly rewards.
In whatever place he is born, he always dwells among the noble and honored;
though he experiences the utmost worldly glory, he does not give rise to deep attachment,
but only aspires to the path that is supreme among the supreme.
Having no other thoughts whatsoever—
this is the fourth vow.
